### 🔩 Materials (Steel, Aluminum)

 Tariffs on raw materials are handled separately — often 25–50%
 Automotive-specific tariffs usually override metal tariffs to prevent double taxation (“destacking” rules) [...] It varies. While the base rate for many countries is still 25%, new trade deals have reduced rates for some — including 15% for the EU and Japan, and 10% for select UK vehicles. Other countries like China face 30% or higher.

### Are car parts also taxed under the 2025 tariffs?

Yes. A 25% tariff applies to most imported auto parts, unless they are USMCA-compliant or fall under a specific exemption. This affects engines, electronics, brake systems, and more. [...] Example: A Chinese brake rotor taxed at 25% steel tariff will not be taxed an additional 25% as an auto part

### 🛠️ Exceptions for Essential Replacement Parts

Select categories of parts used for maintenance and safety repairs may receive exemptions — especially:

 Brake systems
 Airbags
 Headlights and lighting modules

Exemptions are granted through a petition process and apply only to direct replacements for vehicles already on U.S. roads.

results.title: Importing Auto Parts Into the US: Classification Determines Your Section 232 Tariff Rate - Dedola Global Logistics
results.content:
The Section 232 tariff on auto parts is a 25% duty, added in 2025, that applies only to a defined list of HTS-classified components rather than to auto parts as a general category. Covered categories include: ● Engines and engine parts (HTS 8407, 8408, and 8409) ● Vehicle bodies and chassis (HTS 8706 and 8707) ● General parts and accessories under HTS 8708, including bumpers, brakes, gearboxes, axles, wheels, suspension components, radiators, exhaust systems, clutches, steering components, and [...] The 25% stacks on top of your existing duty rate. It doesn’t replace it.

 Most HTS 8708 parts already carry a base Most Favored Nation duty rate between 0% and 4%.
 Brake components under HTS 8708.30, for example, carry a 2.5% MFN rate on their own.

Section 232 adds to that. For example:

| Shipment | Base MFN duty | Section 232 | Combined |
 ---  --- |
| $50,000 of brake components (HTS 8708.30) | $1,250 (2.5%) | $12,500 (25%) | $13,750 (27.5%) | [...] If your parts come from Canada, Section 232 isn’t the only tariff action to track anymore. Two more recently took effect, and they don’t follow the same rules.

Section 301 added a forced-labor enforcement duty on imports from a list of countries that includes Canada and Mexico, an additional 10% on top of existing rates. It exempts two categories:

 Goods already subject to the Section 232 tariff.
 Goods that qualify for the USMCA exemption.
